title: 2. What the Company Does: Segments, Revenue Mix & Concrete Examples

epigraph.quote: Hedgers transfer risk they cannot afford to carry; speculators absorb risk in search of return. The exchange collects a tiny toll on both sides of the handshake.
epigraph.author: Commodity Market Microstructure

web_blocks.html: MCX runs a two-sided electronic exchange and central clearing house for non-farm commodity derivatives in India. It holds over 99% domestic market share across bullion, energy, and base metals [12]. Unlike a commodity trader or warehouse firm, MCX takes zero price risk on gold, crude oil, or copper. Instead, it charges a fee per lakh of turnover on every futures and options trade matched on its book [1][13][14]. It also earns interest on clearing cash float (other income), annual member and port fees, and market data sales [1][13][14].

In FY26, MCX posted ₹2,302 crore in operating revenue, up 107% YoY from ₹1,113 crore in FY25, plus ₹127 crore in other income [1][13]. Commodity Options drove the bulk of sales at ₹1,398 crore (+109% YoY, ~60.7% of operating revenue) [1][13]. Commodity Futures added ₹693 crore (+136% YoY, ~30.1% of operating revenue) [1][13]. The rest—~₹211 crore (~9.2%)—came from member, terminal, data, and clearing fees [1][13]. By Q2 FY27, quarterly operating revenue hit ₹800 crore (₹1,502 crore in H1 FY27) [1][11]. Options notional Average Daily Turnover (ADT) surged 225% YoY to ₹12,00,129 crore, or ₹10,291 crore in options premium ADT [1][11]. Futures ADT reached ₹62,819 crore (+50.6% YoY) in the same quarter [1][11].

web_blocks.takeaway: Options earn roughly 2x the revenue of futures on MCX. Fees are ₹41.80 per lakh on option premium—nearly 20x the ₹2.10 per lakh futures rate. That makes option premium velocity the main profit driver.

web_blocks.html: Three real-world examples show how MCX's toll-booth works across its core markets:

web_blocks.title: Concrete Real-World Customer Examples Across MCX's Three Pillars
paragraphs: 1. Bullion Jeweller & Refiner (Futures Hedging): A Mumbai jeweller holds 10 kg of gold stock ahead of the wedding season. To guard against a sudden price drop before retail sales close, the jeweller sells 10 MCX Gold (1 kg) futures contracts—or 100 Gold Mini (100g) contracts for finer sizing—via a clearing broker [3]. Suppose spot gold falls ₹2,000 per 10 grams. The physical stock loses ₹20 lakh, while the short MCX futures trade gains ~₹20 lakh in daily MCXCCL settlement, wiping out price risk [5]. MCX earns ₹2.10 per lakh on both entry and exit [14].

2. Retail / Prop-Desk Options Trader (Energy Volatility): A prop desk or active trader on a discount broker expects a sharp move in NYMEX-linked WTI crude ahead of a US stock report. Rather than posting full futures margin, the trader buys out-of-the-money MCX Crude Oil Mini options for a small premium [4]. MCX charges ₹41.80 per lakh strictly on the premium value, not the notional strike value [14]. Fast intraday turnover in crude and natural gas options thus drives high fee yield per rupee of trader capital [14].

3. Industrial Metal Fabricator & Power Consumer (Base Metals & Electricity): A cable maker bidding on a 9-month power grid job locks in input costs with far-dated MCX Copper futures out to 12 months [11][19]. Alongside industrial smelters, it can also hedge power-cost swings using MCX's new Electricity Futures, which hit ₹77 crore ADT in Q2 FY27 [11][19].

web_blocks.html: Under SEBI's July 2024 'True-to-Label' rule, effective October 1, 2024, MCX ended volume-slab rebates [6][14]. It moved to a flat fee of ₹2.10 per lakh on futures and ₹41.80 per lakh on options premium [6][14]. This regulatory shift did not hurt MCX's fee yield or net realization. Instead, active F&O client counts grew 90% YoY to 14.98 lakh in Q2 FY27, lifting fee revenue smoothly [11]. Meanwhile, treasury interest on clearing float added ₹127 crore in FY26 and ₹52 crore in Q2 FY27, giving MCX a steady second income stream [1][10].

book_paragraphs: Strip away the financial jargon, and MCX is a digital tollbooth sitting at the intersection of India's physical commodity economy and global price discovery. It does not mine gold, drill for crude oil, or store copper ingots in its own warehouses. It builds the electronic order book, guarantees every trade through its wholly owned clearing corporation MCXCCL, and charges a tiny, regulated toll every time a buyer and seller shake hands.

The real magic—and the reason you and I need to watch the product mix closely—lies in the difference between futures and options. In FY26, MCX earned ₹693 crore from commodity futures and ₹1,398 crore from commodity options, out of ₹2,302 crore in total operating revenue. Why do options generate twice the revenue of futures? Because under MCX's flat 'True-to-Label' fee schedule implemented in October 2024, futures pay ₹2.10 per lakh of contract value, whereas options pay ₹41.80 per lakh of option premium. Whenever volatility rises in gold, silver, crude oil, or natural gas, option premiums expand and traders turn over those contracts rapidly—multiplying MCX's revenue yield.

Let's ground this in three real-world people using the exchange today. Picture a mid-sized jeweller in Mumbai sitting on ten kilograms of gold ahead of Diwali. If international gold prices drop overnight, the jeweller's inventory loses lakhs of rupees. By shorting MCX Gold futures, any loss on the physical gold is offset rupee-for-rupee by gains on the exchange contract. Next, picture a quantitative prop desk or retail options trader watching weekly US crude inventory data on a discount broker app. Instead of tying up large margin in futures, they trade Crude Oil options, paying a small premium on which MCX collects ₹41.80 per lakh. Finally, picture a copper cable manufacturer bidding on a year-long infrastructure tender: with MCX extending base metal futures out to twelve months—and even launching electricity derivatives that hit ₹77 crore in daily turnover in Q2 FY27—industrial hedgers can lock in both metal and power costs on one platform.

Add to that ₹127 crore of FY26 other income earned largely on MCX's own reserves and cash collateral parked at MCXCCL, and you see why this is a remarkably clean, two-engine business: transaction tolls on volatility and risk transfer, plus steady treasury yield on the clearing float.

book_callouts.title: NARRATOR'S REFLECTION: Notional vs. Premium Turnover
book_callouts.text: Media headlines love quoting MCX's ₹12 lakh crore options notional turnover in Q2 FY27 because the number sounds astronomical. As a disciplined analyst, you should always look straight past notional turnover to options premium turnover—₹10,291 crore per day in Q2 FY27—because MCX bills its ₹41.80 per lakh fee strictly on premium, not notional value.

book_subsections.title: Decoding the Fee Schedule: Futures vs. Options Economics
paragraphs: If you want to read MCX's quarterly revenue like an insider, start with one crucial distinction: futures and options are billed on completely different bases, and their fee rates differ by nearly twenty-fold. Under SEBI's July 2024 'True-to-Label' circular—implemented on October 1, 2024—MCX eliminated volume-based slab rebates and adopted a clean, flat tariff. Commodity futures are billed at ₹2.10 per lakh of contract turnover value, whereas commodity options are billed at ₹41.80 per lakh of option premium turnover.

That single structural difference explains why options now dominate MCX's top line. In FY26, total operating revenue more than doubled (+107% YoY) from ₹1,113 crore to ₹2,302 crore. Commodity options delivered ₹1,398 crore (+109% YoY, or roughly 60.7% of operating revenue), while commodity futures contributed ₹693 crore (+136% YoY, or 30.1%), with the remaining ₹211 crore (9.2%) coming from membership, terminal, data, and ancillary clearing fees. By Q2 FY27, operating revenue hit ₹800 crore in a single quarter (₹1,502 crore for H1 FY27). Even though headlines trumpeted ₹12,00,129 crore in options notional Average Daily Turnover (+225% YoY), you and I know the real billing engine was the ₹10,291 crore in options premium ADT—alongside ₹62,819 crore in futures ADT (+50.6% YoY)—across 14.98 lakh active F&O clients.

book_subsections.title: Walkthroughs Across Bullion, Energy, Base Metals & Electricity
paragraphs: To see how this two-sided marketplace serves real participants, let's trace three everyday users across MCX's core pillars. First, consider a Mumbai bullion jeweller holding 10 kilograms of physical gold ahead of the wedding season. If global gold prices drop ₹2,000 per 10 grams before retail buyers walk in, that inventory loses ₹20 lakh in value. By selling 10 contracts of MCX Gold (1 kg) futures—or 100 contracts of Gold Mini (100g) for finer sizing—through a clearing broker, the jeweller locks in a ~₹20 lakh mark-to-market gain via MCXCCL that offsets the physical loss, while MCX collects ₹2.10 per lakh on both entry and exit. Across bullion, Gold Mini, Gold Ten, Silver 100g (which crossed ₹100 crore ADT in Q2 FY27), and BULLDEX options drove a 496% YoY surge in bullion ADT in FY26.

Second, picture a proprietary trading desk or active retail trader via a discount broker positioning around weekly US crude inventory releases. Instead of posting full futures margin, the trader buys out-of-the-money Crude Oil Mini options for a modest premium outlay; high-frequency intraday turnover in crude and natural gas options feeds directly into MCX's ₹41.80 per lakh premium toll. Third, picture a copper cable manufacturer bidding on a nine-month power grid tender. By buying far-dated MCX Copper futures (extended up to 12 months, alongside 18-month crude contracts and a relaunched Nickel contract) and hedging power-cost swings via MCX's newly launched Electricity Futures—which captured ~75% market share at ₹77 crore ADT in Q2 FY27—industrial hedgers can manage both metal and energy exposure under one roof.

book_subsections.title: The Second Engine: Treasury & Clearing Float
paragraphs: Notice what MCX does not do: it never takes directional price risk on gold, crude oil, copper, or electricity. Every long contract on the order book is matched against a short contract, and MCXCCL stands in the middle solely as central counterparty. Alongside transaction tolls, MCX's second revenue engine is treasury yield earned on its own reserves and the substantial cash collateral parked by clearing members at MCXCCL. That float generated ₹127 crore of other income in FY26 (up from ₹98 crore in FY25) and ₹52 crore in Q2 FY27 alone (₹102 crore in H1 FY27), providing a steady, high-margin earnings cushion regardless of daily trading swings.
